title: Aligning & communicating benefits
blurb: Explain why benefits must line up with strategic objectives, and choose the right way to communicate them to each stakeholder.
question: A housing association is building a repairs app. The board wants to know how it supports the strategy, tenants want to know what changes for them, and repair operatives are worried about their workload. Why must the app's benefits be aligned with strategic objectives, and how should they be communicated to each group?

teach.h: A clear line of sight to strategy
teach.body: Projects exist to deliver organisational strategy. ALIGNING benefits means each benefit can be traced to a strategic objective it contributes to. In plain English: if someone asks 'why are we spending this?', you can point from the project, through its benefits, to a goal the organisation has already agreed matters. Benefits that can't be traced this way are hard to justify and easy to cut.

teach.caption: Each benefit sits under an objective the board has already agreed. That traceability is what 'alignment' means.

items: It justifies the investment: the business case can show what strategic goal the money serves.
It guides prioritisation: portfolio boards select and rank projects by strategic contribution.
It keeps support: sponsors and senior stakeholders back work that advances their goals.
It shows when to stop: a project whose benefits no longer fit a changed strategy can be closed.
It focuses scope: requirements traced to benefits, and benefits to objectives, cut 'nice to have' work.

rows.label: Board support
values: Weak: seen as a side project

rows.label: Benefits reviews
values: Measure what the board cares about

head: Method
Best for
rows: The investment decision and the strategic fit
Showing how outputs lead to benefits and objectives
Regular forecast updates for the sponsor and board
Explaining what changes for a particular group
Making early benefits real and building support
Formal evidence of what has been realised
teach.caption: No single method suits everyone. Choose by audience, purpose and timing.

teach.h: Tailor the message to the audience
teach.body: Stakeholder analysis tells you what each group needs. The board wants strategic contribution and financial return in a concise form. Users want to know what's in it for them and what changes day to day. Operational managers want the impact on workload and performance. The same benefit can be framed three ways without changing the facts. Be honest about dis-benefits too: hidden bad news destroys trust faster than anything.

teach.h: Matching benefits communication to power and interest
teach.caption: The power/interest grid from stakeholder analysis helps decide how much detail, how often and through which channel.

teach.body: The board gets a monthly dashboard showing first-time fix rate and cost per repair against targets, tied to the two strategic objectives. Tenants get a newsletter story: 'Mrs Patel's boiler fixed in one visit'. Operatives get briefings on fewer wasted trips and less paperwork, plus an honest note that the first month will feel slower while they learn. Because the app is built iteratively, early releases produce real results to share within weeks, not years.

teach.text: Communicating OUTPUTS is not communicating BENEFITS. 'The app went live on 3 June' is an output message; 'repairs fixed first time rose from 70% to 85%' is a benefits message. Also beware options that send everyone the same report or hide dis-benefits to protect the project: both are wrong.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Explain alignment: each benefit traces to a strategic objective it supports.
Give reasons: justifies investment, guides prioritisation, keeps support, shows when to stop.
Name several communication methods: business case, benefits maps, dashboards, reports, briefings, success stories, reviews.
Explain tailoring: different stakeholders need different content, detail and channels.
Add an example matching a method to a stakeholder, such as a dashboard for the board.
Alignment: every benefit traces to a strategic objective it contributes to.
Why: justifies investment, guides portfolio prioritisation, keeps support, flags projects to stop.
Methods: business case, benefits maps and profiles, dashboards, progress reports, briefings, success stories, benefits reviews.
Tailor content, detail and channel to each audience, using stakeholder analysis.
Communicate benefits, not just outputs, and be open about dis-benefits.

summary: You can now explain why benefits must align with strategic objectives and what goes wrong when they don't. You can also choose suitable ways to communicate benefits and tailor them to different stakeholders.

A.q: What is the main reason for aligning a project's benefits with strategic objectives?
options: It lets the project manager own every benefit
It shows the spend serves organisational goals
It removes the need to review the business case
It guarantees the outputs will be on schedule
A.why: Alignment shows how the project's benefits contribute to agreed strategic objectives, which justifies the investment.

whyNot.0: Benefits are owned by the sponsor and benefit owners, and alignment doesn't change that.
whyNot.2: The business case still needs regular review, especially if strategy changes.
whyNot.3: Alignment concerns value, not delivery performance against the schedule.

A.q: A board member has high power but little interest in project detail. Which is the BEST way to communicate benefits to them?
options: A weekly email listing every task completed
A full copy of the benefits register daily
An invitation to every team stand-up
A concise dashboard of benefits vs targets
A.why: High power, low interest means 'keep satisfied': short, strategic, at-a-glance information such as a benefits dashboard.

whyNot.0: Task lists are output detail this stakeholder doesn't want.
whyNot.1: A daily full register overloads a low-interest stakeholder.
whyNot.2: Stand-ups are for the delivery team, not senior stakeholders.

A.q: A portfolio board must choose between two projects with similar costs and risks. Which should it favour?
options: The one with the most outputs to deliver
The one whose benefits best fit strategy
The one with the longest delivery period
The one led by the most senior manager
A.why: Portfolio prioritisation selects projects by their contribution to strategic objectives.

whyNot.0: More outputs doesn't mean more value.
whyNot.2: A longer schedule delays benefits; it isn't a reason to prefer a project.
whyNot.3: Seniority of the manager doesn't measure strategic contribution.

B.q:
Which TWO of the following are ways of communicating a project's benefits?
1) A benefits map
2) A resource histogram
3) Success stories
4) A critical path network
options: 1 and 3
2 and 3
1 and 4
2 and 4
B.why: Benefits maps show how outputs lead to benefits and objectives; success stories make early benefits real for stakeholders.

whyNot.1: A resource histogram shows resource loading, not benefits.
whyNot.2: A critical path network shows schedule logic, not benefits.
whyNot.3: Neither a histogram nor a network diagram communicates benefits.

B.q: Midway through a project, the organisation's strategy shifts away from the market the project serves. What does this mean for its benefits?
options: They still count, as they were approved
They are now the PM's problem to solve
Their alignment must be re-checked now
They should be reported less often
B.why: If strategy changes, benefits may no longer contribute to objectives, so alignment (and the business case) must be re-checked; the project may need re-planning or closing.

whyNot.0: Approval was based on the old strategy; it doesn't guarantee continued value.
whyNot.1: The sponsor owns the business case and benefits; the PM flags the impact.
whyNot.3: Reducing reporting hides the problem instead of dealing with it.

B.q: Why should the way benefits are communicated be tailored to each stakeholder group?
options: Groups differ in what they need and value
It lets the project hide its dis-benefits
It cuts the number of benefits to track
It means the sponsor needs no reports
B.why: Different groups have different interests, influence and information needs, so content, detail and channel should differ.

whyNot.1: Tailoring is about relevance, not concealment; dis-benefits should be communicated honestly.
whyNot.2: Tailoring changes how benefits are presented, not how many are tracked.
whyNot.3: The sponsor still needs regular benefits reporting.

C.q: A council's digital parking project tells residents only that 'the new system went live on 3 June'. Residents stay hostile. What would MOST improve the message?
options: Sending the same message much more often
Adding more technical detail on the system
Asking the supplier to send it out instead
Showing what's better for them, with proof
C.why: The message is about an output. Residents need to hear the benefit to them, backed by evidence, to build support.

whyNot.0: Repeating an output message doesn't answer 'what's in it for me?'.
whyNot.1: Technical detail suits specialists, not residents.
whyNot.2: Changing the sender doesn't fix the content.

C.q: Which is NOT a benefit of aligning project benefits with strategic objectives?
options: The investment can be justified to the board
Projects can be ranked in the portfolio
Benefits no longer need owners or measures
Senior support for the project is kept
C.why: Alignment doesn't replace good benefits management: every benefit still needs an owner, measure, baseline, target and timing.

whyNot.0: Justifying investment is a core reason for alignment.
whyNot.1: Alignment is what lets the portfolio prioritise projects.
whyNot.3: Senior stakeholders support projects that advance their goals.

C.q: A benefits review finds a dis-benefit: older residents face longer waits during changeover. How should it be communicated?
options: Openly, with the fix, to those affected
Only to the board, to protect the project
Not at all, until it has been resolved
Only in the project's risk register
C.why: Dis-benefits should be communicated honestly to those affected, with the mitigation, to keep trust and manage expectations.

whyNot.1: Hiding it from those affected damages trust when they discover it.
whyNot.2: Silence leaves affected people without information or support.
whyNot.3: A register entry isn't communication with the stakeholders affected.

reteach.title: New floodlights at a community football club
reteach.question: A football club's committee wants to grow junior football. It spends £60,000 on floodlights. How does it show the floodlights are aligned with its goal, and how should it talk about the benefits to different people?

blocks.body: The club's strategy is 'more juniors playing'. The floodlights (output) allow winter evening training (outcome), which means 40 more juniors registered (benefit). That's the line of sight. To the committee: registrations and subs income against target. To parents: more sessions after school, all year round. To the council that part-funded it: community participation figures. Same benefit, three framings.

blocks.text: 'The floodlights are installed' is an output message. Nobody funds floodlights for their own sake; they fund what the lights make possible.

explain.body: Each benefit should trace upward to a strategic objective it contributes to. If it can't, the project's value is hard to justify and easy to cut.

test.q: A project benefit can't be traced to any strategic objective. What is the MAIN risk?
options: It will be much easier to measure
It may not justify investment
It will be realised sooner
It will need fewer owners
test.why: Without a link to strategy, it's hard to show the investment serves the organisation, so the benefit may not justify the cost.

whyNot.0: Alignment doesn't affect how easy a benefit is to measure.
whyNot.3: Every benefit still needs an owner.

explain.body: Alignment justifies investment, lets portfolio boards prioritise, keeps senior support, and signals when a project should stop because strategy has moved on.

test.q: In portfolio management, how is benefits alignment MAINLY used?
options: To schedule the team's daily tasks
To allocate the team's desks
To select and prioritise work
To choose the contract type
test.why: Portfolio management selects and prioritises projects by how well their benefits serve strategy.

whyNot.0: Task scheduling is done within each project.
whyNot.3: Contract type is chosen in the procurement strategy.

explain.body: Business case, benefits maps and profiles, dashboards, progress reports, stakeholder briefings, success stories and benefits reviews. Each suits a different purpose.

items.label: progress vs targets at a glance

test.q: Which tool shows, on one page, how outputs lead to benefits and on to strategic objectives?
options: A Gantt chart
A RACI chart
A change request log
A benefits map
test.why: A benefits map links outputs, outcomes, benefits and strategic objectives visually.

whyNot.0: A Gantt chart shows the schedule.
whyNot.2: A change log records change requests.

explain.body: Use stakeholder analysis to adapt content, detail, language and channel. Boards want strategic and financial value; users want what changes for them; managers want impact on performance.

test.q: Frontline staff are anxious about a new system. Which benefits message suits them BEST?
options: How it will make their daily work easier
The project's return on investment figure
The portfolio's list of strategic priorities
The supplier's reimbursement arrangements
test.why: Frontline staff care most about what changes for them day to day, so that is the benefit to lead with.

whyNot.1: ROI suits the board, not anxious frontline staff.
whyNot.2: Portfolio priorities are too remote from their concerns.
whyNot.3: Contract payment terms aren't relevant to them.
